evidence.quote: The self-study covers our own projects and is dominated by one project, which contributes 42% of events; the latency result comes from a synthetic repository on one machine; and the client suite is small and partly single-run.

No measure of prevention. The evaluation shows that memory accumulates and that the gate is cheap in the measured synthetic workloads; it does not show that the gate prevents repeated failures, which requires the benchmark proposed below.
The hand-edited project map can drift from the implementation, the git hooks and watcher rely on unvalidated heuristics, and library-name matching can misattribute cross-project lessons (Section 4).
The gate is only as good as the logged history; on a new project it has little to report, which backfilling from git history mitigates but does not remove.

No semantic recall. projectmem deliberately performs no vector retrieval, trading fuzzy recall for determinism and zero read-time model cost; it complements rather than replaces embedding-based memory.

Summary growth. Notes are capped in the projection, but issues and standing decisions are not, so the summary grows with a project’s history. In one of our own long-lived projects, with 101 standing decisions, it reached roughly 120,000 characters, on the order of 30,000 tokens, well above the session-start estimate of Section 4.
The gate’s thresholds are engineering defaults whose utility has not been evaluated.
Secret redaction is pattern-based and fail-open, so it can miss a secret in an unfamiliar format and, if the scrubber fails, lets an event through unredacted.

Complete supersession. Resolving chains of references by traversal, presenting a retired decision alongside its replacement rather than withholding it, detecting two decisions that retire the same target, and a token-budgeted projection that keeps the session-start read fixed as a project ages.
